cues.text: A Reformer's Eye for Truth
By the middle of the eleventh century, Peter Damian had already become one of the Church’s most formidable reforming voices.
He was prior of the hermitage of Fonte Avellana in central Italy and a tireless critic of clerical corruption and simony.
A man not given to credulity or exaggeration, he would go on to be honored as a Doctor of the Church precisely for the rigor and honesty of his writing.
This same disciplined witness left behind, in his own hand, one of the more carefully documented Eucharistic accounts to survive from the medieval Church.
It was not a legend gathered generations later, but a report from a man present, or very near, to the events he described.
A Theft at the Altar Rail
In the year 1050, Peter Damian's own account relates, a woman gave in to what he called a horrible temptation.
Urged on by a sorceress who wished to put the consecrated host to some forbidden use, she hid it in a handkerchief during Holy Communion rather than receive it.
She turned at once for the door of the church.
A priest who had noticed what she had done pursued her before she could leave, caught her, and demanded that she return what she had taken.
Half Flesh, Half Bread
Peter Damian records that, when the priest unfolded the linen cloth in which the host had been wrapped, he found it transformed.
No one present could explain away the change: one half of the host had visibly become flesh, while the other retained the plain appearance of bread.
Peter Damian himself drew out the meaning he believed God intended by so partial and pointed a sign.
He wrote simply of the event: "This is a Eucharistic event of great importance."
To his mind, transforming only half the host demonstrated that ordinary-looking bread held the same reality as what had visibly become flesh.
He believed this lesson was aimed at unbelievers who denied the Real Presence outright.
Preserved in the Saint's Own Words

Unlike many medieval Eucharistic accounts that reach us only through later retellings and shrine pamphlets, this one survives in Peter Damian's own theological writing, later collected among his works in the Patrologia Latina.
That does not make every circumstantial detail beyond question.
The identity of the woman, the sorceress, and the exact parish are not independently corroborated elsewhere.
But it does place the account, as sourced material, well ahead of most medieval Eucharistic traditions in documentary reliability.

No continuously venerated physical relic from this specific account is known to survive to the present day; its value lies chiefly in Peter Damian's own theological reading of what he says he witnessed.
Legacy
Peter Damian's account differs from many later medieval Eucharistic traditions.
It is not primarily a wonder meant to draw pilgrims, but a theologian's own testimony, offered as evidence in his broader defense of orthodox belief against his age's doubts and errors.
He would go on to spend his life confronting corruption within the Church with the same unflinching honesty he brought to this single, carefully recorded episode.
For believers who wrestle today with doubts of their own about what happens upon the altar, Peter Damian's witness offers something quieter than spectacle.

It is the testimony of a rigorous, reforming mind who saw no contradiction between demanding intellectual honesty of the Church and kneeling in awe before what he believed God had shown him with his own eyes.
